sections.overview: The Eurasian curlew is the largest European wading bird, known for its long, down-curved bill and its bubbling, far-carrying call over moorland and estuaries. It is now a species of high conservation concern, with steep declines across much of its range.
sections.identification: A curlew measures 50–60 cm, with a wingspan around 90 cm, and weighs roughly 770 g to 1 kg; females are larger than males and have longer bills. The plumage is mottled brown and grey, the legs long and bluish, and in flight a white wedge shows on the rump. The smaller Whimbrel (Numenius phaeopus) has a shorter bill and a pale crown stripe; the larger Far Eastern Curlew (N. madagascariensis) has a dark rump. See their profiles for the reciprocal comparisons.
sections.habitat: In the breeding season in Britain it is most frequent on moorland and also common in marshes, using upland rough pasture, heather moor, bogs and wet grassland. In winter it moves to the coast and nearby farmland, with the highest densities on major estuaries.
sections.diet: It finds worms, shellfish and shrimps by probing the ground with the sensitive tip of its long bill. It pinches the prey and often tosses it into the air before swallowing, because its tongue cannot reach far enough to move it.
sections.behavior: Its “cur-lee” and bubbling calls are heard over breeding grounds from February to July. From July many birds move to the coast, where they roost in flocks at high tide and feed on the mudflats at low tide. British winter flocks are joined by migrants from Fennoscandia.
sections.reproduction: In Britain the first clutch is laid on average around 2 May, typically four eggs, with one brood. The female, and occasionally the male, incubates for 27–29 days. The downy chicks run soon after hatching and fledge after 32–38 days. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.
sections.ecology: Nest predation is a major problem: egg predation caused nest failure in up to 97% of nests in a Northern Ireland study in the 1990s, and foxes were the main cause in a Breckland study. Predator control raised success in one Northumberland site, though the effect of some predators appears to depend on the place. Changing farm practices and loss of breeding and chick-rearing habitat also contribute to the decline.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists the species as Near Threatened. The UK breeding population was about 59,000 pairs in 2016 and fell by 51% between 1995 and 2024; the UK is thought to hold over 30% of the west European population, and the species is Red-listed in the UK. A curlew typically lives about 11 years once adult, and the oldest ringed bird reached over 32.
